answer.answer: Chevron completed the acquisition of independent oil and gas exploration and production company Hess Corporation on July 18, 2025 [1]. The aggregate purchase price of Hess was approximately $48 billion, which included open market purchases of Hess common stock and Chevron common stock issued as closing consideration [2]. As part of the transaction, Chevron assumed debt with an aggregate outstanding principal value of $8.8 billion [2]. Hess’s principal upstream operations are located in the United States, Guyana, and Malaysia, along with an approximately 38 percent ownership interest in Hess Midstream LP [2][1]. Chevron notes that the success of the acquisition depends on its ability to realize anticipated benefits, such as run-rate cost synergies and five-year production and free cash flow growth rates [3].

citations.quote: On July 18, 2025, the company acquired Hess Corporation (Hess), an independent oil and gas exploration and production company. Hess’s principal upstream operations are in the United States, Guyana and Malaysia. Hess’s operations also include an approximately 38 percent ownership interest in Hess Midstream LP (HESM), with operations primarily in the Bakken shale in the Williston Basin area of North Dakota.

The aggregate purchase price of Hess was approximately $48 billion, including 15.38 million shares of Hess common stock purchased in open market transactions in the first quarter of 2025 and 301.25 million shares of Chevron common stock issued as closing consideration in July. As part of the transaction, the company assumed debt with an aggregate outstanding principal value of $8.8 billion.

The success of the acquisition of Hess, which closed in July 2025, will depend, in part, on Chevron’s ability to realize the anticipated benefits, including the anticipated run-rate cost synergies, estimated five-year production and free cash flow growth rates, and anticipated higher returns to shareholders over the long-term.

The accrual balance aligns with the Company's best estimate of its share of a probable and reasonably estimable loss regarding the U.S. covered litigation, though this estimate could materially vary based on litigation developments [3].
